title: Reconguista in G's Gundam Base Exclusive G--Self Perfect Pack Gets Rare Online Release for Gundam Winter Fest 2026 - Essential Japan
content: A Gundam Base-exclusive version of the G-Self Perfect Pack is now available online for a limited time, with the movie-inspired Gunpla kit joining Bandai’s latest major promotional event. The “HG 1/144 THE GUNDAM BASE LIMITED G-SELF PERFECT PACK (Reconguista in G the Movie Ver.)” joins more than 200 Gunpla kits and related accessories available through Premium Bandai US for Gundam Winter Fest 2026, including a selection of normally store-exclusive Gundam Base models. G-Self first appeared in the 2014 anime Gundam Reconguista in G, which followed Bellri Zenam, a young Capital Guard cadet who became the pilot of the mysterious Mobile Suit during a conflict involving several competing factions in the Regild Century. Directed by Gundam creator Yoshiyuki Tomino, the series later received five theatrical compilation films released between 2019 and 2022, featuring revised animation, additional scenes, and changes to the original story. The G-Self Perfect Pack appeared during the latter stages of the story, combining equipment and capabilities associated with the Mobile Suit’s various backpack configurations into a single powerful system. Its specialized equipment allowed Bellri to switch between several combat modes, including the devastating Photon Torpedoes used during the conflict’s final battles. Bandai originally released the Gundam Base-exclusive High Grade kit in October 2024, introducing an updated version of the G-Self Perfect Pack based on its appearance in the theatrical films. The model builds upon the original “HG 1/144 Gundam G-Self (Perfect Pack Equipped)” from 2015, incorporating newly molded components across the head, chest, shoulders, and joints to improve its proportions, detailing and articulation. One of the most significant changes is the redesigned head, which more closely recreates the G-Self’s appearance in the movies, including its larger eyes that are recreated by new plastic stickers, revised sensors, and improved separation of the different armor colors. Its chest has also received substantial changes, including a newly molded transparent cover and improved detailing around the Beam Saber storage compartments. Additional articulation has been incorporated into the neck, shoulders and waist, allowing the upper body to bend and rotate more freely than the original High Grade release. The hip joints now feature a sliding mechanism that increases the range of movement in the legs, while adjustments to the elbows and knees provide greater flexibility for combat poses. The completed model retains the G-Self’s familiar blue, white and red coloring, with the transparent sections and updated stickers recreating the glowing Photon Battery details across its body. Its most prominent equipment is the Perfect Pack, a large backpack that combines several of the G-Self’s specialized systems through articulated binders, movable thrusters, and deployable weapons. The backpack supports multiple configurations, including Atmospheric Mode and Space Mode, with its equipment repositioned to recreate the different capabilities used throughout the story. Assault Mode can also be reproduced by extending the backpack’s weapon assemblies and adjusting the positions of its Traffic Fins, giving the G-Self a more heavily armed appearance. The kit also includes special effect parts for Reflector Mode, allowing builders to display the backpack’s energy-deflection equipment in its deployed configuration. Additional weapons include the Towasanga-produced Beam Rifle, Photon Armor Shield, and two Beam Sabers, with interchangeable hands provided for different combat poses. An Action Base 7 is included with the Gundam Base edition, providing additional support for the completed model and its large backpack during airborne displays. Builders can also assemble the G-Self without the Perfect Pack attached, with the kit including the necessary components to reproduce its standard Mobile Suit appearance. Another Gundam Base-exclusive kit available during Winter Fest is the “MG 1/100 Zaku Cannon (Z Gundam Ver.)”, which recreates the Earth Federation-operated Zaku Cannon from Mobile Suit Zeta Gundam with its alternative blue and purple coloring. That Master Grade is currently accepting limited-time US pre-orders through the same promotion, providing another opportunity to purchase a normally store-exclusive Gundam Base model online. Gundam Winter Fest 2026 runs from November 6 at 5:00 PM PST until November 30 at 11:59 PM PST, temporarily offering a large selection of Gunpla kits, Gundam Base limited models, and building accessories through Premium Bandai US. The “HG 1/144 THE GUNDAM BASE LIMITED G-SELF PERFECT PACK (Reconguista in G the Movie Ver.)” is currently in stock for $49, although quantities may be limited and the kit could sell out before the promotion concludes. Premium Bandai US also offers free shipping on qualifying orders over $99 independently of Gundam Winter Fest, so builders purchasing the G-Self Perfect Pack can add other eligible kits or accessories to reach the required threshold. title: Why BMW Middleweights Might Be The Smartest ADV Buys In 2026 - Top Speed
content: Abhik has been an automotive journalist for over 14 years, with expertise in both motorcycle and car road testing, reviewing, as well as writing and executing feature travelogs. His written work has been published in leading Indian automotive magazines, including Evo India Magazine, Auto Today (India Today Group), and he has anchored video reviews for the televised Auto Today Show on the India Today channel, as well as Powerdrift Studios on YouTube. He also has keen interests in most forms of motorsports, having competed in a couple of seasons of one-make racing with TVS Racing on two wheels and Volkswagen Motorsport on four. Alongside his motoring pursuits, e-sports and sim racing are his current interests, as are cycling and cycling tech. Adventure bikes are meant to traverse the world, enabling the rider to conquer just about any terrain and still be able to ride it to work with barely a fuss. This means doing opposing jobs, so simply buying the biggest one isn’t the straightforward solution for everyone. The biggest ADVs are like large off-roaders that come on their own in the right environment, but in the city and urban landscape, they’re quick to feel misplaced. BMW’s boxer-powered R 1300 GS models remain the flagships, yet the middleweight range now covers what makes an ADV genuinely useful. For many riders in 2026, the better buy may be the GS that gives up unnecessary excess. Let’s start with weight, because the middleweight label can be misleading in this class. A smaller engine does not guarantee a lighter motorcycle once fuel, protection, and touring equipment are slapped on. A 20 or 30-lb difference can also disappear quickly beneath the added bulk of luggage. Weight only becomes a major advantage when the whole motorcycle is designed around reducing it or, at least, not making it felt. Cost is more straightforward. A lower entry point leaves money for luggage, tires, protection, training, or simply more riding. It can also make taking the bike onto a rocky trail feel less financially intimidating. A scratch on a brand new 1300 GS on a tight trail where it’s unavoidable is going to hurt much more than a lower-priced equivalent. And adventure riding is a space where expensive bodywork and hard ground meet pretty often. An ADV also needs enough power to cruise, pass traffic with luggage, and handle elevation, but hitting the dirt and the loose terrain rarely needs huge horsepower. In fact, more power is detrimental to better bike control on the dirt. Throttle response, gearing, traction, and rider confidence become more useful tools as grip drops. A middleweight can therefore surrender substantial peak output without losing real adventure capability. All of this, however, only works if the chassis suits the job. A road-biased bike use should not make its owner tolerate a tall rally setup every day, while a dirt-focused model should not carry additional touring hardware bulk that it may not ever need. BMW intelligently avoids asking one middleweight GS to cover all of this and instead bifurcates the duties onto three distinct 2026 F-series motorcycles. The F 800 GS, F 900 GS, and F 900 GS Adventure share BMW’s 895cc parallel-twin, but they are not merely three equipment grades. The F 800 GS makes 87 horsepower and 67 pound-feet, while both F 900s produce 105 horsepower and 68.6 pound-feet. BMW then changes wheels, suspension, fuel capacity, ergonomics, weight, and equipment around that engine. One is road-biased, another is built to spend more time in the dirt, and the third GS adds the necessary hardware for longer tours. At $10,995, the F 800 GS is the cheapest and most approachable of the trio. Its 32.1-inch seat, 19-inch cast front wheel, 4.0-gallon tank, and 500-lb road-ready weight suit commuting, pavement, poor roads, and easier gravel sections more than any technical off-road riding. The 87 horsepower tune still has enough performance for interstate riding and luggage carrying, but without making the motorcycle needlessly aggressive. Heated grips, ABS Pro, Dynamic Traction Control, a 6.5-inch TFT, and two riding modes come standard. For riders who frequently leave the pavement seeking the off-the-beaten-path, the $14,395 F 900 GS is the key model. It gets a 21-inch cross-spoke front wheel, 9.05 inches of front travel, an adjustable 43 mm fork, wider enduro footpegs, and a 34.2-inch seat height, yet weighs 482 pounds ready to ride. Its 3.8-gallon tank limits the range, but the smaller plastic tank contributes to a broader weight-saving solution over the old F 850 GS. If rough terrain is the priority, carrying less fuel can be preferable to carrying unnecessary mass through every difficult section. The F 900 GS Adventure proves why displacement is a poor proxy for size. At 542 lb, it is 19 lb heavier than the standard R 1300 GS, so this is not a lightweight boxer alternative by any means. Instead, $15,195 buys a 6.0-gallon tank, adjustable touring screen, comfort seat, aluminum engine guard, luggage rack, and the same 105-horsepower parallel-twin. Its purpose, however, is to package touring hardware below flagship money. Its natural comparison is the R 1300 GS Adventure. That bike brings 7.9 gallons, shaft drive, 145 horsepower, 110 pound-feet, and more technology, but weighs 593 pounds and starts at $23,795. The F 900 GS Adventure is 51 pounds lighter and $8,600 cheaper while retaining a 21-inch front wheel and more than nine inches of front suspension travel. The standard R 1300 GS complicates the comparison because BMW has kept its weight under control. At 523 pounds, it is only 41 pounds heavier than the F 900 GS, while offering tech like the Telelever front suspension, cruise control, and electronics. The F 900 GS nevertheless saves $6,000, enough to materially change the ownership proposition. The question is not whether the boxer offers more, but how often a rider will use what the extra money buys. The F 800 GS appeals to its buyers for different reasons. It is only 23 pounds lighter than the R 1300 GS, so its case rests on its lower seat height, friendlier road-biased nature, and a huge $9,400 lower MSRP rather than drastic mass reduction. These are differences that matter every day, and not only on an ambitious trip. Yamaha’s 2026 Ténéré 700 starts at $10,999, almost exactly beside the F 800 GS, but its 21-inch front wheel and 689cc platform give it a stronger dirt bias. Riders who prioritize trail work may prefer the Yamaha by default. That makes the F 800 GS better suited to riders whose adventures include substantial pavement use, and that’s what should dictate the choice. The 2026 KTM 890 Adventure R puts similar pressure on the F 900 GS with its $16,299 MSRP, 21/18-inch wheels, 9.45 inches of suspension travel, and roughly 474 pounds fully fueled weight, making it the harder-core off-road tool. However, BMW’s strength in 2026 is the space it leaves between those extremes. Across the three F-series GS models, BMW has effectively separated price, ergonomics, and intended terrain use instead of pretending that displacement solves all three use cases in one unified high-power package. title: Royal Enfield Himalayan 750 vs BMW F 450 GS Spec Comparison: What's Different? - Times Now
content: Royal Enfield Himalayan 750 and BMW F 450 GS compared. (AI-generated Image) The new Royal Enfield Himalayan bike is all set to enter the adventure segment in India. As the market is flooded with multiple options across different engine capacities and features, choosing the right one could be tough. One of its major rivals, the upcoming Himalayan 750, is the BMW F 450 GS, which has a smaller engine and a comparatively lighter package. The Himalayan 750 gets a 743cc parallel-twin engine, while the BMW F 450 GS comes with a 420cc parallel-twin unit. So, how do the two adventure bikes compare in terms of design, performance, hardware, and features? Let's take a look. The Royal Enfield Himalayan 750 comes in five colour options: Antarctic Silver, Siberia White, Viking Bronze, Aztec Green and Tectonic Black. The BMW F 450 GS, in contrast, is available in four variants with three distinct colour schemes. The Base and Exclusive variants come in Cosmic Black, while the newly introduced Sport variant adorns a Racing Red colour. The higher-spec GS Trophy variant is offered in Racing Blue Metallic with red and white accents. The F 450 GS has a 420cc liquid-cooled parallel-twin unit that makes 48hp and 43Nm at 8,750 rpm and 6,750rpm, respectively. It also has a six-speed transmission. The Himalayan 750 has the upper hand in displacement and torque. BMW offsets the lower displacement with a lighter overall package, giving the F 450 GS an advantage in terms of power-to-weight ratio. Both Royal Enfield and BMW Motorrad have opted for a 19-inch front wheel and a 17-inch rear wheel on their respective adventure bikes. That said, the major differences lie in wheel types rather than sizes. The former offers both cast-alloy and tubeless spoke-wheel options, while the latter gets cast-alloy wheels as standard. But it allows buyers to choose rugged cross-spoke wheels as a factory add-on. In comparison, the F 450 GS packs rider-assistance systems, including engine brake control, DTC, and ABS Pro. Buyers can also opt for heated grips, while the GS Trophy variant comes with BMW's Easy Ride Clutch (ERC). It features a 6.5-inch TFT screen. Royal Enfield has not disclosed the Himalayan 750 price in India yet. The motorcycle recently made its debut at EICMA 2026, and the India launch is expected at Royal Enfield's Motoverse 2026 edition. title: Gen.G Breaks Semifinals Jinx, Reaches First Final Since Rebranding - 조선일보
content: Gen.G Sweeps Invictus Gaming 3-0, Sets Up Potential LCK Clash With T1 in Finals Desperation paid off. Gen.G finally broke the frustrating Worlds semifinals jinx and earned a chance to challenge for the world title. Gen.G, the No. 1 seed from LCK (Korea), swept Invictus Gaming (IG) from LPL (China) with a 3-0 set score in the semifinals of the '2026 League of Legends World Championship' (Worlds) held on November 8 (Korea time) at the Credit Union of Texas Event Center in Allen, Texas, USA, securing a spot in the finals. This marks Gen.G’s first appearance in the Worlds final since its rebranding from Samsung Galaxy at the end of 2017. Previously, Gen.G had reached the semifinals four times—2021, 2022, 2024, and 2025—but failed to overcome the final hurdle at Worlds, losing three times to LCK teams and once to an LPL team. Although Gen.G proved its international competitiveness by reaching the summit twice at the MSI (Mid-Season Invitational), it had yet to claim the prestigious Worlds championship trophy. As a dominant force representing LCK, winning Worlds was both a long-standing ambition and an essential milestone. The victory over IG completed a dramatic "four failures, fifth success" story, marking Gen.G’s first-ever advance to the finals after four previous semifinal exits. The match itself was dominant. In the first set, Gen.G seized the initiative with a 33-minute victory led by the stellar performance of 'Canyon' Kim Gun-bu. In the second set, Gen.G showcased even more flawless gameplay, overwhelming IG with a one-sided kill score of 26 to 9, demonstrating superior skills in both offense and defense. The third set was different. Gen.G struggled until the late game against a fierce counterattack from IG, pushed to the brink. However, Gen.G’s focus shone in the decisive moment. Around the 39th minute, they swept four kills in a final team fight, reversing the momentum and destroying IG’s nexus for a shutout victory. Gen.G’s finals opponent will be either T1, LCK’s archrival aiming for a fourth consecutive Worlds title, or LPL’s BLG, which is riding a strong upward trend. The two teams will face off in a best-of-five semifinals match at the same venue on November 9. If T1 defeats BLG, the Worlds final will feature the first-ever "Gen.T1" clash, a historic showdown between two LCK powerhouses vying for the world championship. In this scenario, LCK would also achieve a record-breaking 11th overall Worlds title. BLG is no easy opponent, however. While they showed some instability with a 3-2 record in the Swiss Stage, they swept LCK’s Diplus GIA 3-0 in the quarterfinals, gaining momentum. Their resurgent form in the knockout stage makes them a formidable challenge for T1. Staff Reporter Nam Jung-seok bluesky@sportschosun.com

title: Buick Is Still Building Sleek Sedans, Just Not for America - AOL.com
content: Buick last sold a sedan in the U.S. in 2020, when the Regal was discontinued. Since then, the brand has been selling only crossover SUVs in its home market, but things are quite different in Buick’s largest market—China. Buick currently sells four different sedans in China—Verano, Regal, Electra L7, and LaCrosse—and a fifth one will soon join their ranks. Buick is bringing back the Electra GS name in the guise of a sleek-looking plug-in hybrid sedan. Inspired by last year’s Electra GS Concept, the production model looks less striking, as it often happens when a design study reaches the production stage, but it’s still an eye-catching design. The first photos of the new Buick Electra GS come courtesy of China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (via CarNewsChina), which periodically publishes regulatory filings on upcoming automotive products. As you can see in the images, the Electra GS has a more traditional sedan shape than the 2025 concept, although the fastback roofline and smooth surfaces are still there. The plug-in hybrid sedan features slim headlights that wrap around a trim piece stretching across the front end; the element can be had either in body color or in silver. A similar trim piece is found at the rear flanked by the LED taillights and a light bar that spans the entire width of the car. Unlike the concept that featured flush door handles, the Electra GS features semi-hidden door handles to comply with the current safety legislation in China. The front bumper also has a gaping grille at the bottom, while the rear features an aggressive-looking lower bumper with two trim pieces sticking out on each side and flanking the license plate area. From a size standpoint, the Buick Electra GS measures 196 inches in length, which places it in Audi A6 territory. It’s around two inches shorter than the Electra L7, another sedan sold by Buick in China with battery electric and extended range electric powertrains. The GS is also 1.5 inches narrower and has a 5.3-inch shorter wheelbase than the L7. The Electra GS uses a plug-in hybrid powertrain consisting of either a 97-horsepower naturally aspirated 1.5-liter four-cylinder gas or a 154-hp turbocharged 1.5-liter. Each of the gas engines is paired with a front-mounted 221-hp electric motor powered by a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack. Since both the ICE and the electric motor are placed on the front axle, all Electra GS variants are front-wheel-drive-only. The more powerful variant enables a top speed of 118 miles per hour. The battery capacity is not yet available, but the filing does note that there are two different suppliers for it: Rept Battero Energy and Zenergy. Built jointly with GM’s joint-venture partner SAIC, the Electra GS will enable Buick to compete with popular models like the BYD Qin L DM-i (known as the Seal 6 in Europe) and Geely Galaxy L6 in the Chinese market. Pricing and full specifications will be announced closer to the model’s launch. Since we’re talking about a model developed and built in China with software developed specifically for Chinese consumers, it goes without saying that Buick couldn’t sell the Electra GS in the United States even if it wanted to. title: Buick’s Newest Sedan Has A GS Badge, But Isn’t For America - CarBuzz
content: Many automakers have different lineups for different regions, but one brand with arguably the most divergent lineups is Buick. In the US, we know it for upscale SUVs from subcompact to full-size, and they're all fairly conventional. You won't find any major electrification in any American Buick. Over in China, though, you can get SUVs, sedans, and even minivans with the brand, and you'll find all manner of hybridization and even full electric power. Now, Buick's Chinese division is about to get another hybrid in a sleek sedan package, and it has us wondering what's taking so long for American hybrids. This latest hybrid is another in the Electra line of cars, and it adopts the GS suffix that has long adorned Buick's highest-performance models. The brand hasn't officially introduced the model, but thanks to details being published by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, we get an early (and extremely clear) look at it. It's a clean-looking thing with a nice low nose and a fastback roofline. Close examination of the rear shows a shut line that goes around the rear glass, suggesting it's a liftback, rather than a true sedan. It also has slim wraparound LED lighting at the front and back, and the diffuser section of the rear bumper reminds us a bit of the Porsche Taycan. While svelte, the Electra GS also looks a bit anonymous, as it follows the Chinese car design trend of going basically grille-less, but also not doing much with the front and rear fascias. The documents do show optional contrasting silver panels for the front and rear that add at least a bit of visual interest. The photos also show cameras on the fenders, and a lidar sensor on the roof. These won't be standard, though. Other images show roof and fender designs without driver assist components. Because of all the specifications included in the government documents, we also know how big the Electra GS is. It's 196 inches long, and it has a wheelbase of 112.8 inches. It's almost identical in size to the Toyota Crown, though its a little more than an inch shorter than Toyota's tall sedan. Despite the name, the Electra GS won't be much of a sports sedan. The documents show that it will be a plug-in hybrid, and at least one version of the car will feature a turbocharged 1.5-liter four-cylinder making 154 horsepower. It should also make 170 pound-feet of torque assuming it's the same engine that's used in the Electra E7 SUV. The electric motor is gutsier, making 221 horsepower, and, assuming the E7 connection, 243 pound-feet of torque. On the E7, Buick lists combined power and torque, but it simply adds the peak numbers together, which doesn't necessarily give an accurate picture of just how much propulsive power is provided. We would assume combined power is somewhere near the electric motor's output. It's adequate, but far from exhilarating. CarScoops reports that a base model will also be available with the lower-output powertrain from the E7. It uses a naturally-aspirated 1.5-liter four-cylinder making 97 hp and 96 pound-feet of torque. In the E7, that engine is still paired with the same 221-hp electric motor. Being a plug-in hybrid, the Electra GS will be able to charge up from the grid and operate fully electrically. Assuming that the powertrains are taken directly from the E7, it should get the same 32.6-kWh battery pack as the SUV. On China's test loop, that provides 146 miles of range. That would absolutely be lower on the US test cycle, but that's still a sizable battery and would likely provide plenty of range. The GS will probably go even further on a charge thanks to being more aerodynamic. Just like every other Chinese Buick, with the sole exception of the Envision, it's all but guaranteed the Electra GS won't come to America. Tariffs on Chinese vehicles, plus the cost of safety and emissions certification, on top of being a less-than-popular body style in our market make it a non-starter. Although it's possible it could show up in other markets, maybe even as close as Mexico, since Buick is looking to bring more of its Chinese models to other markets. The fact that Buick has added another hybrid to its already extensive roster does raise the question of what's taking so long for GM to bring hybrids back to the US. Emissions certification and production locations would be the main hindrances, just as it would be for a complete vehicle. GM does have hybrid plans for the US, though, as it's pouring money into a Michigan facility to build hybrid powertrains in the next few years, likely for its full-size SUVs that could include Buick's own Enclave. title: BMW F 450 GS Sport Launched At Rs 5.90 Lakh - DriveSpark
content: The BMW F 450 GS Sport has been launched in India at Rs 5.90 lakh (ex-showroom). The F 450 GS Sport is the fourth variant of the middleweight adventure motorcycle from BMW Motorrad and it comes with Sport Suspension and an exclusive Racing Red finish. Until now, the F 450 GS was sold in Base, Exclusive and GS Trophy variants. The new Sport slots in between the Exclusive and the GS Trophy, and is Rs 25,000 more affordable than the top-spec Trophy variant. When the BMW F 450 GS first went on sale in April, the Base was priced at Rs 4.70 lakh, the Exclusive at Rs 4.90 lakh and the GS Trophy at Rs 5.30 lakh. Prices have gone up since, and the range now starts at Rs 5.35 lakh. (All figures mentioned are ex-showroom). The new BMW F 450 GS Sport variant uses the same 420cc liquid-cooled parallel-twin as the rest of the range. The engine pushes out 48bhp at 8,750rpm and 43Nm at 6,750rpm through a 6-speed gearbox. BMW quotes an unladen weight of 178kg and a seat height of 845mm for the F 450 GS. Sport Suspension is the headline change in the BMW F 450 GS Sport, giving the ew variant a more focused setup than the standard Base and Exclusive variants. Gear Shift Assistant Pro is also standard, allowing clutchless gear changes under the right conditions. Riding Modes Pro adds an Enduro Pro setting to the existing Rain, Road and Enduro modes. Both the Sport and the GS Trophy get Sport Suspension and Riding Modes Pro. The Trophy adds BMW's Easy Ride Clutch, which isn't listed for the Sport, so the BMW F 450 GS Sport relies on a conventional clutch backed by Gear Shift Assistant Pro. The Trophy also has an aluminium engine guard and a tinted Rallye windscreen. With the arrival of the BMW F 450 GS Sport riders who wanted the Trophy's equipment without the Easy Ride Clutch now have that option. Racing Red paint is exclusive to the Sport. The X-shaped LED headlamp, front beak and upright proportions carry over from the other variants. title: Lee So-young's return keeps the "Four Attackers" alive; IBK Industrial Bank of Korea defeats defending champion GS Caltex to secure second consecutive win [V-League] - 스타뉴스
content:
Hwaseong IBK Industrial Bank of Korea extended its winning streak to two games by also defeating "defending champion" Seoul GS Caltex. IBK Industrial Bank of Korea defeated GS Caltex with a set score of 3-1 (28-26, 25-19, 25-27, 25-21) in the home game of the women's division of the 2026-2027 HK Hieunguk Financial V-League held at Hwaseong Comprehensive Gymnasium on the 6th. IBK Industrial Bank of Korea, which won against Suwon Hyundai E&C in the opening match on the 3rd, rode a rising momentum by also defeating GS Caltex, who had topped both last season's championship and the Cup tournament. GS Caltex suffered a loss after its first win. For IBK Industrial Bank of Korea, foreign main attacker Victoria Danchev (registered name: Victoria), who recorded the highest points among both teams, scored 25 points; middle blocker Choi Jung-min, who blocked six times, contributed 23 points; another middle blocker Lee Ju-ah added 17 points; and outside hitter Osanai Miwako (registered name: Miwa) chipped in with 14 points. Unforced errors reached 24, more than Hyundai E&C (16), and IBK did not hold a significant advantage in blocks (15-12). There was also no major difference in serves (4-3) and attack success rate (39.53%-34.62%). The difference between the two teams was decided by attack efficiency (29.07%-19.87%), which hinged on defense, including serve reception. At the center of this was the returning ace, Lee So-young. Lee So-young, who transferred to IBK Industrial Bank of Korea with a total compensation of 700 million won ahead of the 2024-2025 season, could not play in many matches due to injury. Her shoulder injury worsened further next season, leading her to undergo surgery last November. Lee So-young, who felt an immense burden of failing to justify her market value, requested contract termination from the club. She could not become a "bailout" (a player who leaves after receiving high compensation). As a high-earning player, she was determined to reduce the club's financial burden while returning only when she was in a definite physical condition. Although she is still not at 100% physical condition, Lee So-young is contributing significantly to defense with a diligent attitude. Of the six points she scored on this day, three were from attacks, three were blocks, and the rest were contributions from defense. Her reception efficiency reached an impressive 62.29%. This was much higher than libero Im Myeong-ok (33.33%), and she even succeeded in 19 digs, more than Im Myeong-ok (18). Lee So-young solidly guarded the back row alongside Im Myeong-ok, providing a foundation that allowed setters to distribute the ball with confidence. Kim Ha-kyung and Park Eun-seo increased the utilization frequency of Victoria (usage rate 32.56%), Miwa (23.26%), as well as Choi Jung-min (18.6%) and Lee Ju-ah (17.44%), shaking up GS Caltex's defensive line. This also became a factor that lowered the attack efficiency of GS Caltex's main attacker Silva to 15.52%. IBK Industrial Bank of Korea, which was leading 23-20 in the first set, faced the danger of losing the set after conceding four consecutive points, but ultimately forced a deuce and took the first set with a score of 26-26 thanks to Silva's consecutive unforced errors. In the second set, despite committing as many as 10 unforced errors, IBK held on stably, with Lee So-young recording a 100% reception efficiency. Kim Ha-kyung utilized various attack routes and secured another win with efficient attacks. IBK Industrial Bank of Korea, which narrowly lost the third set after a deuce, widened the score gap in the fourth set starting with Lee So-young's quick open point. Through bold attacks enabled by Lee So-young's stable reception, they extended the lead, and with Lee So-young's block also hitting its mark, they stretched the score from 7-7 to 12-8. They then maintained their lead consistently to ultimately secure the victory. In the men's division match held at Incheon Gyeoyang Gymnasium, Suwon KEPCO staged an upset by defeating Incheon Korean Air, who achieved a double title last season, with a set score of 3-1 (25-23, 18-25, 26-24, 27-25). The difference was decided by concentration in crucial moments. KEPCO created a set point at 23-23 in the first set with an open attack by Sharon Vernon Evans (registered name: Sho), and took the first set on Korean Air's hit error. After losing the second set, KEPCO was trailing 23-24 in the third set when Yoon Ha-jun scored a quick open point and then smiled after recording two consecutive service aces. In the fourth set, they were again in danger at 23-24, but KEPCO entered a deuce with Sho's back attack and decorated the victory with Lee Min-gyu's block and Sho's finishing touch. KEPCO, led by Sho with 26 points and Yoon Ha-jun with 14 points in team attacks, secured one win after one loss. title: Karol G’s Ex Anuel AA Says She Still Has Him Blocked on Social Media - AOL.com
content: Anuel AA said he was joking about asking Karol G to unblock him on social media and hasn’t actually done it The former couple ended their two-year engagement in 2021 after first meeting on a music video set Karol G previously said her album Mañana Será Bonito helped her heal after their split Karol G is seemingly keeping her social media ex-free. On Friday, Nov. 6, Anuel AA sat down with Billboard to discuss his upcoming music —and he was asked about his relationship with a superstar ex. In the past, the Puerto Rican rapper has publicly discussed that Karol has him blocked on social media. While promoting his song “Vuelve” (Spanish for “return”) in October, Anuel wrote a plea for his ex in the caption. “RETURN KAROL G. UNBLOCK ME BB. IT’S NOT THAT I’M A PLAYER. IT’S THAT I FALL DEEPLY IN LOVE,” he wrote on Instagram in Spanish. In his interview with Billboard, Anuel was asked if he had seriously asked her to unblock him yet. “No, I’m just messing with her. But maybe she’ll unblock me,” Anuel said. When asked if he wishes for all of his exes to be at peace with him, he said “not all of them.” “We should live in peace, right?” he said, adding that if a movie was made about his love life, it would be called Anuel’s Love’s a Bitch. “It’ll sell a lot. It’ll be incredible.” Anuel — who’s gearing up to release Real Hasta La Muerte 2 (RHLM 2) and a Mexican corridos album this month — and Karol first met in 2018 on the set of their “Culpables” music video. The pair went on to announce they were dating in November 2018 and announced their engagement in April 2019. After a two-year engagement, Anuel and Karol called it quits in April 2021, announcing their breakup on social media. “If just accepting it is hard enough, imagine having to do it in front of millions of people,” Karol wrote in Spanish on her Instagram Story at the time. “For a long time we tried to keep our relationship away from social media in order to protect ourselves. We never used our relationship for marketing purposes, not today, not even almost three years ago when we started [dating].” Months after they ended their engagement, Karol and Anuel reunited on stage at the end of her Bichota Tour and the “Tusa” singer said she would “always admire” him on social media afterward. In July 2024, Karol told PEOPLE that her fourth studio album, Mañana Será Bonito, was her attempting to “heal my heart” from their split.

title: The Adventure Bike That Makes Owning One Motorcycle A Boss Move - Top Speed
content: Motorcycle marketing often promotes the belief that true versatility demands a multi-bike stable: a light thumper for trails, a midweight twin for commuting, and a heavy rig for touring. Managing multiple registrations, insurance policies, and maintenance schedules turns that ideal into an expensive burden. Yet experienced riders know extreme specialization often sacrifices basic usability. Sitting quietly at the premium end of the adventure segment is an understated machine commanding a devoted following because it handles city traffic, cross-country highway miles, and backcountry gravel roads with equal poise, rendering a multi-bike garage unnecessary. The modern full-size adventure segment suffers from a chronic identity crisis, caught between desert-rally marketing and the tarmac reality of long-distance touring. To substantiate rugged off-road claims, manufacturers fit long-travel suspension and 21-inch front wheels to platforms that spend 90 percent of their lives on pavement. On asphalt, that geometry yields vague front-end feedback, slow steering, and crosswind instability. Simultaneously, taming these tall chassis at highway speeds requires massive curb weight and invasive electronics to mask the packaging compromises. Riders face an irritating trade-off: machines too detached and wallowy for spirited cornering, yet far too heavy and intimidating for low-speed technical terrain. Solving this dynamic compromise requires packaging substantial displacement without saddling the motorcycle with a tall roll center. This top-heavy pendulum effect is common to tall V-twin and inline adventure platforms. Placing heavy components as close to the ground as possible dramatically reduces turning inertia. BMW mastered this specific physical balance through its horizontally opposed boxer twin. By positioning the cylinder heads flat and low, BMW drops the core mass beneath knee level, delivering light low-speed handling, straight-line stability on washboard roads, and fatigue-free highway touring. The BMW R 1300 GS gets respect everywhere it goes, because it proves why smart mechanical packaging eliminates the need for separate motorcycles. Combining an ultra-compact boxer layout, under-engine gearbox, and low-slung chassis,it replaces three specialized machines with one integrated platform all for a base price of $20,395. With the optional automatic gearbox, the price climbs to over $25,000, but it manages to be fatigue-free even in traffic. It strips away top-heavy intimidation while retaining all-day touring comfort, establishing itself as the definitive one-bike solution. BMW's 1,300 cc engine looks to be on track to be one of the greats, with its German engineering mastery. It has liquid cooling, four valves per cylinder, BMW ShiftCam on the intake valves that changes both timing and lift, an extremely short stroke design, and a high compression ratio of 13.3:1. It generates 145 horsepower at 7,750 RPM and 110 pound-feet at 6,500 RPM, and it has a six-speed manual transmission with an assist-and-slipper clutch. A two-way quickshifter is optional, but the automated manual gearbox (also optional) is what makes it a genuinely great all-round motorcycle. A driveshaft sends power to the rear wheel, which is great for low-maintenance operation. Unlike its competitors, the R 1300 GS uses a unique chassis. This is a pressed-steel monocoque that uses the engine as a stressed member, and the subframe is bolted on. It uses the Evo Telelever wishbone front suspension that offers 7.5 inches of travel and the Paralever central monoshock at the rear with a single-sided swingarm that offers 7.9 inches of travel. Twin 310 mm floating brake discs do duty up front with radial four-piston calipers, and a 285 mm disc at the rear with a two-piston floating caliper. These are mounted on alloy wheels — a 19-inch up front and a 17-inch at the rear — with radial tubeless tires. Tubeless wire-spoke rims are an option, as are more aggressive off-road tires, so you can configure it to feel right at home on any road. The R 1300 GS is a full-size adventure motorcycle, at 87.1 inches long and 39.4 inches wide with a 59.8-inch wheelbase. The seat height is standard for the class at 33.4 inches, and it has a wet weight of 523 pounds. The fuel tank is pretty large even on the regular GS at five gallons; however, with the weight placed down low, it feels a lot lighter than it is, and this feeling is helped by the electronic suspension as well. The features list is packed with everything you would possibly want from a luxury adventure motorcycle. Hop on, and the first thing you will see is the 6.5-inch TFT instrument cluster that has Bluetooth and navigation as standard. The electronics are comprehensive as well, with a by-wire throttle and a six-axis IMU. Of course, you get ride modes, cornering ABS, traction control, and engine brake control, but the optional extras are what truly elevate the big GS. The optional DSA suspension offers automatic damping control, and you can change the rear preload at the touch of a button. This is also one of the few motorcycles that self-levels with a change in load, and the electronic suspension automatically lowers at walking speeds to make it easier to handle. BMW offers different packages for these upgrades, so you will have to check whether the feature you want is available as a standalone one or as part of a package. Be aware that the packages are quite expensive and will easily drive the price to nearly $30,000. This is the sole thing that works against the GS: the high acquisition cost. Otherwise, it eliminates the need for another motorcycle. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. title: BMW F 450 GS Sport Launch Price Rs 5.90 Lakh – New Colour, Features - BikeAdvice
content: BMW F 450 GS Sport has been launched in the Indian market at a sticker price of Rs 5.90 lakh (ex-showroom, India). It will be the new range-topping variant in the ADV motorcycle’s line-up as untill now, it was offered in Base, Exclusive and Trophy grades at price points of Rs 4.95 lakh, 5.15 lakh, and Rs 5.60 lakh, respectively. The Sport trim has been rolled out in an exclusive Racing Red paintwork with Sport suspension, Gear Shift Assistant Pro and Riding Modes Pro as standard. The new BMW F 450 GS Sport can be purchased at a monthly installment of just Rs 9,999 per month. First things first, the Racing Red colour scheme is flanked by clear Rallye windscreen and black hand protectors. The off-road footrests and plastic engine guard further amplify the adventure character of the new Sport variant. The F 450 GS is available with standard warranty of three years for unlimited kilometers, and it can be extended to fourth and fifth year as an option. Apart from the new features and paint shade, the F 450 GS Sport remains the same in terms of design and engine specs. Sitting on a a welded tubular steel frame with integrated forged parts, it adorns the same iconic ‘GS’ design philosophy with peculiar styling elements such as the ‘X’ shaped full LED headlight, front beak, split-seat setup, tapered aluminum handlebar and body-coloured side panels. The Base and Exclusive variants are available in Cosmic Black Color scheme while the Trophy variant is presented in Racing Blue Metallic with accents in red and white. It flaunts the tank center cover in Snaefell white paint shade while all the other variants have it in matt black colour scheme. Riding on 19-inch front and 17-inch rear lightweight aluminum wheels, the F 450 GS has been fitted with tubeless tires. BMW F 450 GS comes with four ride modes namely Rain, Road, Enduro and Enduro Pro. Some of the notable safety equipment onboard the ADV bike are ABS Pro, Dynamic Brake Control, Dynamic Traction Control and Engine Drag Torque Control. A special mention goes to the 6.5-inch TFT display with multicontroller which gets ‘Pure Ride Screen’ and ‘Sport Screen’ displays. The fuel tank capacity stands at 14 litres while the standard saddle height is pegged at 845 mm. At the heart, the F 450 GS houses the newly developed 420cc twin-cylinder inline engine which generates top power of 47 bhp at 8750 rpm and highest torque of 43 Nm at 6750 rpm. The engine is linked to a 6-speed gearbox. The ADV motorcycle is locally produced at TVS factory in Hosur, Tamil Nadu.

title: ADVENTURE | BMW R 1300 GS PURE - ADB Magazine
content:
There are worse ways to conduct a motorcycle debrief than sitting outside a café with a coffee and a curry pie. Jeremy Cowley had just returned from three solid days of interstate riding aboard BMW’s R 1300 GS Pure, so rather than ask him to sit down and type 2000 words about it, I figured I’d shout him lunch and hit record. Besides, after that many kilometres aboard BMW’s big boxer, his arse had probably spent enough time sitting down. Plus, do you know how hard it is for a journo to get his wallet out! Cowley is becoming our resident adventure-bike tragic whether he likes the title or not. He owns a Husqvarna Norden 901 and a 2006 KTM 950 Super Enduro, has ridden everything from the Royal Enfield Himalayan and Honda CRF300 Rally to the CFMOTO 450MT-X, and there’s plenty more big-bore ADV experience in the family. His old man has owned a Triumph Tiger 800 and now has a Tiger 1200. The GS Pure is an interesting proposition. This isn’t the fully loaded, everything-and-the-kitchen-sink GS most people picture when they hear BMW. It’s the stripped-back entry point into the R 1300 GS family, but it still gets the 1300cc ShiftCam boxer producing a whopping 107kW and 149Nm, along with electronic suspension adjustment, riding modes, a quickshifter, TFT display, keyless ignition and laced wheels. In other words, ‘Pure’ doesn’t exactly mean you’re starting the bloody thing with a kickstarter. So, with coffee in hand and the curry pie rapidly disappearing, I started with the obvious question. JEREMY: Big. And weird. I’ve never really spent much time on BMWs before, so the first thing I noticed was that motor hanging out either side. I’m a massive boxer fan from driving and racing Subarus, so I understand the concept and actually love that engine configuration, but on a motorcycle it’s strange when you’re not used to it. Normally you look down on an adventure bike and see a tank or dual tanks, but on the BMW you look down and there are two bloody cylinder heads sticking out the sides. Once you’re on it, though, it immediately feels like a nice motorcycle. Sometimes with a base-model bike you can tell where the manufacturer has saved money with maybe cheaper bars, slightly ordinary ergonomics or something that makes it feel like the povo-pack version but I didn’t really get that from the Pure. The riding position was comfortable, everything felt quality and after three big days aboard it, I wasn’t looking for an excuse to throw it in a ditch. JEREMY: Bugger me. There is just so much power. It’s that huge wave of torque where you can be cruising along in fourth gear, decide you want to disappear and it just motors. I’ve ridden some seriously fast big adventure bikes now and, for me, the power delivery from this thing was better than any of them. On the road it was beautiful, and I honestly reckon I could ride that thing around Australia. Long highway days, big open roads and huge distances are where that engine makes complete sense because you’ve always got this ridiculous amount of effortless power sitting underneath you. But I reckon it’s almost too much off-road. You’ve got 145 horsepower in an adventure bike and at some point you’ve got to ask yourself what the hell you’re supposed to do with all of it. Nobody needs that much horsepower on a dirt road. Nobody. JEREMY:  I reckon the definition of an adventure bike has changed. On the dirt, I felt like I was having to work for it more than I wanted to. That’s not because the GS is bad; it’s because it’s a massive, hugely powerful motorcycle and this particular Pure isn’t really set up to be a hardcore off-road weapon. It still has plenty of technology to make it manageable, but if I wanted to get serious in the dirt I’d start with tyres and then probably look at the suspension to get it working a little better for that sort of riding. But I don’t think that’s what this bike is trying to be. We’re talking big gravel roads, corrugations, fire trails and stuff where you’re travelling rather than trying to find the nastiest singletrack possible. Put some decent tyres on it and I’d happily point it down that sort of road all day. MITCH: Like a lounge chair you can take down the Oodnadatta Track? JEREMY: Exactly. A really bloody fast lounge chair. JEREMY: No. That boxer engine looks enormous because you’ve got those cylinders hanging out the sides, but all that weight is sitting low. Once the bike is moving it feels much lighter than you’d expect, and when you’re flowing along a road it disguises its size incredibly well. It was probably the nicest adventure-roadie-tourer-whatever-you-want-to-call-it I’ve ridden on the highway. The front-end was another thing. It’s BMW’s Telelever setup and apparently I’m supposed to have some grand opinion on that. Honestly, I didn’t. I probably wouldn’t have mentioned it because there was nothing strange about the way it behaved – it just worked. JEREMY: Fine. The rider triangle felt good sitting or standing and I never really had an ergonomic issue with it. Wind protection was decent too. It’s nowhere near the worst adventure bike I’ve ridden for buffeting although you could fit a bigger screen if you were doing huge touring kilometres. The Pure doesn’t have that giant touring screen, but again, that’s part of what this model is. The only thing that annoyed me was BMW’s scroll-wheel controller on the left grip. I’m not a fan of those systems on bikes generally, so it’s not really a BMW-specific whinge. It works, I just reckon there are simpler ways of doing it. MITCH: ARE BIG-BORE ADVENTURE BIKES BECOMING TOURERS? JEREMY: I think once you get into the 1200 and 1300cc stuff now, you’re really moving towards touring. Look at the bikes around 900cc, you can ride those things all day on the road without a drama, but they’re still bloody capable when you get properly off-road. My KTM 950 Super Enduro is a 2006 model and the 950/990 generation is still regarded by plenty of people as some of the best adventure bikes KTM ever made. It’s funny because the market spent years moving towards 1200 and 1300cc bikes, and now we’re almost coming back around to that 900-ish capacity because it’s such a good compromise. JEREMY: Tyres first, depending on what I was doing. My 950 has a proper aggressive off-road tyre because when I use that bike it’s generally at an event where I know I’m going into the dirt. My Norden 901 has more of a 70/30 tyre because I actually ride it on the road to get places, and when I hit the dirt I’ll drop a couple of psi and get on with it. That’s probably exactly how I’d approach the BMW. If you’re doing 70 per cent bitumen to get to 30 per cent dirt, there’s no point fitting a massive aggressive knob and destroying it at highway speeds before you’ve even reached the fun stuff. The sort of person buying a GS in Sydney, Melbourne or Canberra is probably going to spend a fair chunk of every adventure just getting out of town. JEREMY: Yep. The Pure has Eco, Rain, Road and Enduro modes, and Rain mode is actually really nice on the dirt. It takes the edge off the throttle and gives you some slip without letting the thing completely light up, which isn’t a bad idea when you’ve got a 1300cc boxer trying to fire you at the horizon. Dad used Rain mode quite a bit and I can understand why. A lot of adventure riders do the same thing. You don’t necessarily need maximum aggression just because you’ve left the bitumen; sometimes making a huge motorcycle softer and easier to manage actually lets you ride it faster and with less effort. And that, really, is where we landed once the coffees were empty and Cowley had demolished the pie. The R 1300 GS Pure isn’t pretending to be a 1300cc enduro bike, and perhaps we’ve reached the point where we need to stop expecting enormous adventure motorcycles to be one. Its job is to smash out huge distances in ridiculous comfort, make 145 horsepower feel effortless and let you keep going when the bitumen ends. For that job, Cowley reckons BMW has built a bloody good thing.
